newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: U.S. pledges even hand in Nicaraguan vote.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pledges even hand in Nicaraguan vote.

text.p: The head of a U.S. government delegation monitoring Nicaragua's presidential election said on Saturday the Clinton administration favoured no candidate and would respect the vote's results no matter who won.

"On behalf of the U.S. government, we're not taking sides in this election. We can accept whoever the Nicaraguan people select," Brian Atwood, President Bill Clinton's envoy to the Sunday's elections, told a news conference.
Nicaragua's presidential race pits front-runner Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance against former President Daniel Ortega of the left-wing Sandinista Front.
They are followed by a jumble of 21 lesser candidates.
Earlier this month, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns questioned Ortega's democratic credentials, saying, "We remember the past."

Ortega's Sandinistas fought an eight-year civil war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels in the 1980s that left 25,000 dead. His Marxist rule ended with defeat at the ballot box in 1990 and he now claims to be a moderate social democrat eager to build bridges with the United States.

Throughout much of the 20th century Washington has meddled in Nicaraguan affairs, propping up a dictatorial family dynasty for four decades and seeking to oust the Sandinista government after they seized power in 1979.
"No matter who wins the elections, you're going to have stronger democratic institutions in Nicaragua than before," Atwood said.
If no candidate gets 45 percent of the vote, a runoff will be held for the two top vote-getters in late November or early December.
